newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Generals say Russian army faces collapse.
newsitem.headline: Generals say Russian army faces collapse.

text.p: A group of disgruntled generals opposed to Russian President Boris Yeltsin's military reform said on Monday that his plans threatened the armed forces with collapse.
"We're looking at the full collapse of the armed forces and the liquidation of the country's defence capabilities," General Igor Rodionov, a former defence minister, told a news conference in Moscow.
He said in the face of any military threat, Russia's armed forces were already unable to mobilise, while a dearth of funds meant soldiers were ill-prepared to fight.
"They don't fly, they don't sail, they don't train," said Rodionov.
Yeltsin sacked Rodionov from the defence ministry in May, saying he had dithered in carrying out military reform.

The Russian president followed up last month by restating his plan to cut troop numbers by half a million to 1.2 million by the end of 1998 to streamline Russia's poorly-paid, ill-fed and demoralised army.

Rodionov and other prominent figures in Russia's defence lobby, who have banded together to fight the reforms, say Yeltsin has no clear idea of what kind of army he wants to build and above all, how it should be funded.
"There are a lot of problems but the main problem is money," said Rodionov.
In Soviet times, Cold War exigencies saw the country's military industrial complex -- dubbed the "metal eaters" by Nikita Khrushchev -- get all the guns and rockets it wanted.
But the Cold War's end and Russia's tough journey to the free market have left behind the country's once respected army.

Morale is low among Russia's soldiers and officers, who go unpaid for months and are often forced to live in tents or railway carriages. Their poor condition was made painfully clear by their humiliation at the hands of lightly armed guerrillas in Russia's breakaway republic of Chechnya.

With most of their energy now spent on trying to wring cash out of the government to pay wages and other basic needs, Russia's restive generals say they have little hope of ever matching the United States in military might.
"Stronger than the American army? NATO? It's a lie," Lev Rokhlin, a retired general and head of the lower house of parliament's defence committee, said at the same news conference.

"The factories which produce the weapons we need are standing idle," said Rokhlin, acclaimed for capturing the Chechen capital Grozny in 1995. "Our pilots, submariners and others have not been paid for four to five months," he said.
First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov, quoted by Interfax news agency on Monday, promised that nearly six trillion roubles ($1 billion) in debts to servicemen would be paid out this month.
But Yeltsin's opponents say the armed forces have only received a fraction of their original 1997 budget of 88.3 trillion roubles.
"Yeltsin says not to worry, but nothing's been done in the last two years. We just don't believe him," said Rokhlin, who added that Yeltsin should be impeached.

Last month Yeltsin told the new defence minister, Igor Sergeyev, to launch a publicity campaign to explain the reforms, and gave short shrift to Rokhlin. "We will brush aside the Rokhlinites with their unconstructive actions," the Kremlin leader and commander-in-chief said. ($ = 5800 Russian Roubles)
